subject: Fluid Mechanics
summary: viscous flow between plates and in pipes (Couette and Poiseuille flow, Hagen–Poiseuille), bearings, Stokes' law, and laminar boundary layers (Blasius, displacement and momentum thickness, drag, separation)

questions.text: A 0.5 m × 0.5 m plate is pulled at 0.6 m/s over a 0.4 mm thick oil film resting on a fixed surface, as shown. The force required is 15 N. Assuming a linear velocity profile, the dynamic viscosity of the oil is
solution: Concept: Newton's law of viscosity for a thin film with a linear (Couette) profile: τ = μU/h.
Exam tip: Convert the film thickness to metres first; a missed 10⁻³ gives the distractor 40 or 0.04 × 10³.

questions.text: Oil (dynamic viscosity 0.5 Pa·s) flows in laminar regime between two fixed parallel plates 10 mm apart. The maximum velocity is 0.6 m/s. The shear stress at the plates (in Pa) is ______
solution: Concept: Plane Poiseuille flow: umax = (−dp/dx)h²/(8μ) and τw = (−dp/dx)h/2.
Short cut: τ<sub>w</sub> = μ(du/dy)<sub>wall</sub> = 4μu<sub>max</sub>/h = 4 × 0.5 × 0.6/0.01 = 120 Pa.
Exam tip: Between plates ū = (2/3)umax; in a pipe ū = umax/2. Do not mix them up.

questions.text: Oil flows in laminar regime through a pipe under a fixed pressure difference between its ends. If the pipe diameter is increased by 10 %, the discharge increases by about
solution: Concept: Hagen–Poiseuille: Q = πΔpD⁴/(128μL), so Q ∝ D⁴ at a fixed Δp.
Exam tip: At a fixed Q the head loss scales as 1/D⁴; at a fixed Δp the flow scales as D⁴. 21 % is 1.1², 33.1 % is 1.1³.

questions.text: Oil (density 850 kg/m³, dynamic viscosity 0.1 Pa·s) is pumped at 8 litres/s through a horizontal pipe of 100 mm diameter and 200 m length. Take g = 9.81 m/s². The head loss due to friction (in m, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Check the regime first; if laminar, hf = 32μVL/(ρgD²).
Pumping power = ΔpQ = 522 W.
Exam tip: The same answer comes from Darcy–Weisbach with f = 64/Re; use whichever is faster.

questions.text: A vertical shaft of 200 mm diameter rotates at 400 rpm in a footstep bearing. The end of the shaft is separated from the bearing surface by an oil film 1 mm thick (dynamic viscosity 0.15 Pa·s). The power absorbed in overcoming viscous resistance (in W, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: At radius r the film velocity is ωr, so τ = μωr/t. Torque on a ring: dT = τ(2πr dr)r.
T = ∫₀<sup>R</sup> (μωr/t)(2πr²) dr = πμωR⁴/(2t)
Exam tip: In a journal bearing every point of the film moves at the same speed, so T = τ(πDL)(D/2) directly; a footstep or collar bearing needs the integral because the speed varies with r.

opts: Flow in a circular pipe is usually laminar for Re (based on diameter) below about 2000
The boundary layer on a smooth flat plate usually becomes turbulent at Re<sub>x</sub> of about 5 × 10⁵
In fully developed laminar pipe flow, the Darcy friction factor depends on the pipe roughness
In fully developed pipe flow the velocity profile no longer changes along the pipe
questions.ans: (C) In fully developed laminar pipe flow, the Darcy friction factor depends on the pipe roughness
solution: Concept: In laminar flow the viscous effects dominate and the roughness elements are buried in the slow-moving fluid.
Laminar pipe flow: f = 64/Re, independent of roughness. So (C) is the incorrect statement.
Exam tip: Roughness matters only in turbulent flow (transitional and fully rough zones of the Moody chart).

questions.text: For the boundary layer on a flat plate shown, with δ = boundary-layer thickness, δ* = displacement thickness and θ = momentum thickness, the correct relation is
solution: Concept: δ* = ∫(1 − u/U)dy and θ = ∫(u/U)(1 − u/U)dy; since 0 ≤ u/U ≤ 1, the integrand of θ is smaller than that of δ*, and both are smaller than δ.
Hence δ > δ* > θ, and the shape factor H = δ*/θ > 1 (2.59 for Blasius laminar flow, about 1.3 to 1.4 for turbulent flow).
Exam tip: δ* is the distance by which the wall would have to be displaced outward to carry the same flow in an ideal (inviscid) stream.

questions.text: The velocity profile in a laminar boundary layer is approximated by u/U = 2(y/δ) − (y/δ)². The shape factor H = δ*/θ (round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Integrate with η = y/δ from 0 to 1.
Exam tip: Linear profile: H = 3; parabolic: 2.5; Blasius exact: 2.59.

questions.text: Air (kinematic viscosity 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s) flows at 2 m/s over a smooth flat plate. Using δ = 5x/√Re<sub>x</sub>, the distance from the leading edge at which the laminar boundary layer is 5 mm thick (in mm, round off to the nearest integer) is ______
solution: Concept: δ = 5x/√(Ux/ν) = 5√(νx/U), so x = Uδ²/(25ν).
Check: Re<sub>x</sub> = 17778 < 5 × 10⁵, so the laminar formula applies.
Exam tip: Since δ ∝ √x, doubling the distance multiplies δ by √2 only.

questions.text: A laminar boundary layer exists over the whole length of a flat plate. If the free-stream velocity is doubled (the boundary layer stays laminar), the skin-friction drag becomes
solution: Concept: FD = CD(½ρU²)A with CD = 1.328/√ReL ∝ U−1/2.
So FD ∝ U3/2; doubling U gives 21.5 = 2.83 times.
Exam tip: In laminar flow FD ∝ U1.5L0.5; in turbulent flow (CD ∝ Re−1/5) FD ∝ U1.8L0.8.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT help to delay boundary-layer separation?
opts: Suction of the slow fluid near the wall through slots
Making the boundary layer turbulent with a trip wire or vortex generators
Increasing the adverse pressure gradient by a sharper divergence of the passage
Streamlining the body so that the pressure rises gently
questions.ans: (C) Increasing the adverse pressure gradient by a sharper divergence of the passage
solution: Concept: Separation happens when the near-wall fluid, already slowed by friction, cannot climb an adverse pressure gradient.
Suction removes the slow fluid; a turbulent layer carries more momentum near the wall; streamlining keeps dp/dx small. A sharper divergence makes dp/dx more adverse and promotes separation, so (C).
Exam tip: This is why diffuser half-angles are kept small (about 3° to 4°) and why golf balls have dimples.

questions.text: A sand grain of 0.1 mm diameter (density 2650 kg/m³) settles in still water (density 1000 kg/m³, dynamic viscosity 10⁻³ Pa·s). Take g = 9.81 m/s². Using Stokes' law, its terminal settling velocity (in mm/s, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: At terminal velocity, weight − buoyancy = Stokes drag 3πμVd ⟹ V = (ρs − ρ)gd²/(18μ).
Check: Re = ρVd/μ = 0.90 < 1, so Stokes' law is valid.
Exam tip: Stokes drag means CD = 24/Re; always check Re < 1 before trusting it.

questions.text: In fully developed laminar flow through a pipe, the flow rate is doubled while the flow remains laminar. The Darcy friction factor f and the head loss h<sub>f</sub> become, respectively,
solution: Concept: f = 64/Re ∝ 1/V, and hf = fLV²/(2gD) ∝ (1/V)V² = V.
Doubling Q doubles V: f is halved and hf is doubled.
Exam tip: Laminar hf ∝ V; fully rough turbulent hf ∝ V².

questions.text: Using the von Kármán momentum-integral equation with the linear profile u/U = y/δ for a laminar boundary layer on a flat plate, the boundary-layer thickness is
solution: Concept: τw = ρU² dθ/dx with τw = μU/δ and θ = δ/6.
μU/δ = ρU²(1/6)dδ/dx ⟹ δ dδ = 6ν dx/U ⟹ δ² = 12νx/U
δ/x = √12/√Rex = 3.46/√Rex
Exam tip: Parabolic profile gives 5.48, cubic gives 4.64, Blasius exact gives 5.0 (4.91 to 99 %).

questions.text: Oil (dynamic viscosity 0.8 Pa·s) flows between a fixed lower plate and an upper plate moving at 1.2 m/s, 10 mm apart, with a pressure gradient dp/dx = −1500 Pa/m in the direction of motion, as shown. The shear stress on the fixed plate (in Pa, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Couette–Poiseuille flow: u = Uy/h + (1/(2μ))(−dp/dx)(hy − y²).
du/dy at y = 0: U/h + (−dp/dx)h/(2μ)
Exam tip: A favourable gradient adds to the Couette shear on the fixed plate; an adverse one subtracts and can even reverse the flow near that plate.
